nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{summands} we already know which summands will occur. Hence calculating the multiplicities is all that is required.
nodes.statement_short: Only multiplicities remain

nodes.name: Known multiplicities
nodes.statement: We know the multiplicities of the restriction of the spinor $S_n$; $2$ if $n$ is even, $1$ otherwise. Also, by Lemma \ref{summands} the multiplicities in the restriction of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ are always $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Spinor multiplicities and Lemma (summands)

nodes.name: Compare normalising constants
nodes.statement: Hence, we can find the multiplicities for $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ by comparing $\frac{1}{a_\lambda}$ and $\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}$ from Proposition \ref{alambda}. This is a simple calculation on the eight cases $$\frac{1}{a_\lambda} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ 2\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}& n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1.\\ \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: Compare $1/a_\lambda$ and $1/a_{\lambda^{(i)}}$ in eight cases

nodes.name: Length drop
nodes.statement: Note that $l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1$ occurs once if and only if $\lambda_r = 1$, in which case it is the partition $\lambda^{(r)}$ which has shorter length.
nodes.statement_short: The length drops only for $\lambda^{(r)}$ when $\lambda_r=1$

nodes.name: First part
nodes.statement: The first part can be proved by noticing that, when one forgets the grading, the module $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ is just the parabolically induced module $X_\lambda$, see \cite{BM83}. Hence, one can use Lemma \ref{HOmega} to show how $\Omega_\mathbb{H}$ acts. The constant $( \nu, \nu )$ is exactly the sum we stated.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ with $X_\lambda$ and apply Lemma (HOmega)

nodes.name: Second part
nodes.statement: The second part follows by a simple induction. One can show $\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} (2j - \lambda_i)^2= \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} j(j+1) = \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_k} q(\mathrm{cont}(k,j))$, splitting the cases when $\lambda_i$ is odd or even. This will be covered in more detail in Section \ref{vogan}.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the sum in terms of contents by induction

nodes.name: Chain of equalities
nodes.statement: $$\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}= \frac{1}{4}\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^+ \\ s_\alpha(\beta)<0}} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta $$ $$=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in \Phi^+} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta= \frac{1}{4}(\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}|\alpha|\tau_\alpha)^2$$ $$=\frac{1}{4} (\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\alpha|M_k)^2= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2$$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the Casimir as a square of a sum

nodes.name: Second equality
nodes.statement: In the second equality, we use $\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta = - \tau_\beta \tau_{s_\alpha(\beta)}$ for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $s_\alpha(\beta)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the relation $\tau_\alpha\tau_\beta=-\tau_\beta\tau_{s_\alpha(\beta)}$

nodes.name: Third and last equalities
nodes.statement: The third equality uses the fact that every $\sum_{i=1}^n M_k = \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^+} \tau_\alpha$ and the last equality uses the fact that the Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute in $\mathcal{T}_n$ \cite[3.1]{BK01}. Hence the square of the sum is equal to the sum of the squares.
nodes.statement_short: Sum of $M_k$ equals sum of $\tau_\alpha$; anti-commutation

nodes.name: Induction setup
nodes.statement: We prove the theorem by induction, the base case being trivial. Suppose for every shifted partition $\mu \in \mathcal{SP}(n-1)$, $\mathrm{Scont}(n-1, \mu) = \mathrm{Sspec}(n-1, \mu)$. Let us fix a shifted partition $\lambda$ of $n$, and consider $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ the irreducible representation of $\mathcal{T}_n$ associated to $\lambda$. Let $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n)\in \mathrm{Sspec}(n , \lambda)$. By definition there exists a vector $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_j^2(v_\alpha) =q(\alpha_j )v_\alpha \text{ for all } $j$.$
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $n$; fix $\lambda$, $\alpha\in\mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ and an eigenvector $v_\alpha$

nodes.name: Restrict and use hypothesis
nodes.statement: The restriction of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-1}$ is the direct sum, $\bigoplus_{i =1}^{l(\lambda)} \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$. Also $v_\alpha$ is an eigenvector for the Jucys-Murphys elements. Hence $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ for some fixed $j$. We know, by the inductive hypothesis, $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1}) \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n-1,\lambda^{(j)}) = \mathrm{Scont}(n-1,\lambda^{(j)})$. Explicitly, this means there exists a standard numbering $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]$ of $\lambda^{(j)}$ which corresponds to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Branching plus inductive hypothesis give a tableau for $\lambda^{(j)}$

nodes.name: Two Casimir actions
nodes.statement: Now using Lemma \ref{content}, Lemma \ref{squares} and Theorem \ref{Dirac}, we can describe the action of the Casimir elements of $\tilde{S}_n$ and $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ on $v_\alpha$. Since $v_\alpha$ is in $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ , $$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2 v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_n}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1)v_\alpha. $$ However $v_\alpha$ is also contained in $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}}\subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ so, $$\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} M_k^2v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_{n-1}}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1)v_\alpha.$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute Casimir actions for $n$ and $n-1$

nodes.name: Difference gives $M_n^2$
nodes.statement: the difference of these two Casimir elements is $\frac{1}{2}M_n^2$. Hence $$M_n^2 v_\alpha = \left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1) \right) v_\alpha$$ $$ =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{cont}(k,l)(\mathrm{cont}(k,l)+ 1)v_\alpha,$$ where $(k,l)$ is the block of $ \lambda $ not included in $ \lambda^{(i)}.$
nodes.statement_short: $M_n^2$ acts by $q$ of the content of the added box

nodes.name: Forward inclusion
nodes.statement: Taking the standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]_{(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})}$ associated to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$ and adding the block $(k,l)$ labelled with the number $n$ creates a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\alpha$ of shape $\lambda$. By the above argument this standard shifted tableau has content vector equal to $\alpha \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$. Hence $\alpha \in \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\mathrm{Sspec}\subseteq\mathrm{Scont}$

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: For the reverse direction, we use an almost identical argument. Suppose $\beta =(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_n) \in \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda)$ corresponds to a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. By restriction and inductive hypothesis, there exists a vector $v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_k^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = q(\beta_k) v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})}$. Again using the fact that $M_n^2$ acts by the difference of the Casimir elements $\Omega_{S_n}$ and $\Omega_{S_{n-1}}$, we get, $$M_n^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = 2(\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} - \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}}) = \frac{1}{2}q(\mathrm{cont}(n))v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})},$$ where $\mathrm{cont}(n)$ is the content of the box labelled by $n$ in $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. Hence $\beta \in Spec(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: Same argument gives $\mathrm{Scont}\subseteq\mathrm{Sspec}$

nodes.name: Commutation relation
nodes.statement: One can see that for every $u \in U_\alpha$, $$M_j \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right)u = - \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) M_{s_i(j)}u.$$
nodes.statement_short: Intertwiner swaps $M_j$ and $M_{s_i(j)}$

nodes.name: Identify the image
nodes.statement: Therefore we can conclude that $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha$ is the subspace we labelled $U_{s_i(\alpha)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The image is $U_{s_i(\alpha)}$

nodes.name: Degenerate case
nodes.statement: Note that if $s_i(\alpha) \notin \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ then $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha = 0$ hence, in this case, $\tau_i = \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}$ on $U_\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: If $s_i(\alpha)$ is not in the spectrum the image is zero

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: All we need to show is that the supermodules $V_\lambda$ are isomorphic to $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show $V_\lambda\cong\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$

nodes.name: Agree over JM subalgebra
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{JMsummand} shows that they are isomorphic as $\langle M_1,\ldots,M_n\rangle$-supermodules. The following arguments will show that the action of $\tau_i$ agree on both $V_\lambda$ and $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary (JMsummand): isomorphic over $\langle M_i\rangle$

nodes.name: Case $s_i(\alpha)$ not in spectrum
nodes.statement: If $s_i(\alpha) \notin \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ then Lemma \ref{negative} shows that $\tau_i$ acts on both supermodules identically.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma (negative) gives identical action

nodes.name: Case $s_i(\alpha)$ in spectrum
nodes.statement: In the case that $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} )$ interchanges $V_\alpha$ and $S_{s_i(\alpha)}$ one observes, that applying this operator twice gives $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}\right) ^2 = \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2})\right)Id$$ on $V_\alpha$. Let $p = 1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2} $. Furthermore, again by Lemma \ref{negative} $$\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} P_{s_i}. $$ Rearranging this equation gives the result, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ So again the action of $\tau_i$ is identical on both modules.
nodes.statement_short: Square of the intertwiner is scalar; rearrange to the defining formula

nodes.name: Square of intertwiner
nodes.statement: In the case that $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} )$ interchanges $V_\alpha$ and $S_{s_i(\alpha)}$ one observes, that applying this operator twice gives $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}\right) ^2 = \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2})\right)Id$$ on $V_\alpha$. Let $p = 1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2} $.
nodes.statement_short: The intertwiner squares to $p\,\mathrm{Id}$

nodes.name: Apply Lemma (negative)
nodes.statement: Furthermore, again by Lemma \ref{negative} $$\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} P_{s_i}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Intertwiner equals $-p^{-1/2}P_{s_i}$

nodes.name: Rearrange
nodes.statement: Rearranging this equation gives the result, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ So again the action of $\tau_i$ is identical on both modules.
nodes.statement_short: Recover the defining formula for $\tau_i$

nodes.name: Recall facts
nodes.statement: The set of $V_\lambda$ for shifted partitions is a full set of irreducible representations of $\mathcal{T}_n$. Also $\underline{\zeta}^*(V_\lambda) = \chi_\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: The $V_\lambda$ are all irreducibles and $\underline{\zeta}^*(V_\lambda)=\chi_\lambda$

nodes.name: Translate hypothesis
nodes.statement: So the assumption is equivalent to, for all $\sigma \in \mathrm{irr}(\mathcal{T}_n)$, $\sigma(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}) =(\sigma)(\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}})).$
nodes.statement_short: Hypothesis holds for all irreducibles

nodes.name: Apply density lemma
nodes.statement: Then applying Lemma \ref{density}, $\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma (density) gives equality

nodes.name: Both statements
nodes.statement: The first statement is clear since $Z(\mathcal{T})_{\mathrm{even}}$ is generated by the symmetric polynomials in the squares of the Jucys-Murphy elements. The second statement follows from the fact that every symmetric homogeneous polynomial of odd degree is generated by monomials of power polynomials where there is at least one odd power polynomial.
nodes.statement_short: Even centre generated by $M_i^2$ power sums; odd symmetric polynomials contain an odd power sum

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $\underline{\zeta}$, since it is a homomorphism, will kill any homogeneous symmetric polynomial of odd degree.
nodes.statement_short: Homomorphism kills odd-degree symmetric polynomials

nodes.name: Introduce notation
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots ,\lambda_k)$ be a shifted partition. We are studying the action of power polynomials. Let $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j$ be the $j^{th}$ power polynomial in the $x_i$'s, $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^j$. Let $\chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$-module $St_{\lambda_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes St_{\lambda_k}$ and $\chi_{\lambda_l}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$-module $St_{\lambda_l}$. We consider $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$ to be embedded in $\mathbb{H}$ such that $x_{\lambda_{l-1}+1}, \ldots, x_{\lambda_l}$ are in the image of $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce power sums and parabolic central characters

nodes.name: Decompose $\chi_\lambda$
nodes.statement: Since $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j \in \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$, then $$\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \chi_{\lambda_l} (Q_{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$
nodes.statement_short: Power sum splits over parabolic factors

nodes.name: Decompose $\sigma_\lambda$
nodes.statement: Similarly, for $Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i^j$, $$\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \sigma_{\lambda_l}(Q_{\mathcal{T}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$
nodes.statement_short: Same splitting on the $\mathcal{T}_n$ side

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore if we can prove the result of the theorem for every $\mu = (\lambda_l) \in \mathcal{P}^1$, then using the above decomposition of both $\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j)$ and $\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j)$ we can extend this to $\sigma_{\lambda}$ and $\chi_\lambda$ for every strict $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Length-one case suffices

nodes.name: Setup, base cases and inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Fix $m \in \mathbb{N}$. We prove this statement by induction on $n$ with steps of length two. Note that for $n=0$ and $n=1$, all operators act by zero, hence the base cases are trivial. Suppose the result is true for $n-2$, so: $$\sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n-2)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ in steps of two; trivial base cases $n=0,1$; assume the result for $n-2$

nodes.name: Increment on $\mathcal{T}$ side
nodes.statement: Now, considering that $\sigma_{(n-2)}$ is the restriction of $\sigma_{(n)}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-2}$, $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n}}^{2m}) - \sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \sigma_{(n)}( (2M_{n-1})^{2m} + (2M_{n})^{2m}).$$ By Corollary \ref{actionT} this is equal to \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \sum_{i=1}^{t} (i-1)^m(i)^m - \sum_{i=1}^{t-2} (i-1)^m(i)^m & = (t-2)^m(t-1)^m + (t-1)^m(t)^m\\ & = (t-1)^m ((t-1 + 1)^m + (t-1 -1 )^m ) \\ &= (t-1)^m (\sum_{l=0}^m {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l} (1^l + (-1)^l))\\ & = (t-1)^m\sum_{\substack{l \in {0,\ldots ,m} \\\text{ and even} }} 2 {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l}\\ & = \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Corollary (actionT) and binomial expansion of the increment

nodes.name: Increment on $\mathbb{H}$ side
nodes.statement: We know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m},$$ is just the action of the $x_{t}$ and $x_{t-1}$. Expanding out $P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}$ and explicitly writing $\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m})$ using Lemma \ref{actionH}, we know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m}= \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma (actionH) gives the same increment

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore we have shown that the inductive step holds. Hence $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m})$$ by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step holds; conclude
